title: TB9-14768
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellants XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant, "PA") and her spouse, XXXX XXXX (the male appellant, "MA"), citizens of Hungary, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellants XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant, "PA") and her spouse, XXXX XXXX (the male appellant, "MA"), citizens of Hungary, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection. The appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the negative determination of the RPD and either grant their claim for protection or, refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. They have not submitted new evidence. They have requested an oral hearing.

In June 2015, the appellants initiated a claim for refugee protection at the port of entry. They specifically alleged a fear of persecution in Hungary based upon their Roma ethnicity. They alleged they were the victims of discrimination and escalating incidents of violence, including being threatened and having a Molotov cocktail thrown into their home. They alleged they subsequently relocated from Forro (a small town near Misckolc) to Budapest. However, the incidents of harassment and violence allegedly continued, including being spit at, called anti-Roma slurs, and physically assaulted. The appellants alleged they went to the police, but were told the incidents were not serious and/or that they required witnesses for the police to investigate.
In August 2015, the appellants had their first hearing before the RPD. However, the assigned member's mandate ended without a decision being rendered.
In March 2019, the appellants' de novo hearing was heard by a different RPD member.
In a decision dated May 15, 2019, the RPD rejected the appellants' claim finding the appellants failed to establish their Roma ethnicity.
The appellants argue the RPD made unfounded and unreasonable plausibility assumptions and ignored key evidence (such as police reports).
The appeal is allowed. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the appellants are Convention refugees.
The panel conducted an independent assessment of the evidence to assess whether the RPD decision is correct. THE RPD'S FINDINGS Roma Ethnicity

The RPD determined the appellants failed to establish their identity as Roma. The appellants argue the RPD erred by making unreasonable, cryptic findings and by utterly failing to assess the totality of the evidence. Having independently reviewed the evidence, the panel agrees with the appellants' argument that the RPD erred. In particular, the panel finds the RPD incorrectly focussed on peripheral issues and failed to assess the totality of the evidence.

For example, the RPD drew an adverse inference as to the PA's ethnicity and credibility because of a reference to a university in Portugal on her Facebook page. On this basis, the RPD concluded the PA was not Roma because she must have attended university, "which is inconsistent with what is known to be the general situation of people in Hungary who are of her alleged ethnicity".1 The appellants emphatically deny the PA attended university nor lived in Portugal. They request a hearing before the RAD to confirm the PA's obvious lack of higher education and her credibility in this regard.

As no new evidence has been entered in this appeal, the appellants' request for a hearing is denied. Nonetheless, the RAD agrees with the appellants that the RPD erred. The post on Facebook was not a reliable piece of evidence for the RPD to have given weight. Further, the PA reasonably explained that her friend created the Facebook page for her and might have added details to put her in a better light. Most importantly, the RAD finds the RPD erred in finding that attending university is a marker of ethnicity. It is unequivocally not. The RPD's analysis and finding are therefore wrong and set aside.

The panel has other concerns with the RPD's analysis and findings. For example, the RPD gave no weight to a supporting letter from the Roma Minority Government. The RPD concluded the letter "may be fraudulent" and the "letter can be given no weight as evidence of the claimants' Roma ethnicity".2 The RPD's finding was based upon correspondence from the Hungarian Embassy in Ottawa indicating, "it looks there is no such government in Hungary." The appellants argue the RPD is "absolutely incorrect', as the country documents show there are Roma Self-Governments in Hungary, "which any member would be negligent in not knowing".3

Having independently reviewed the evidence, the panel agrees with the appellants' argument. The panel notes that many different forms of Roma self-governments exist in Hungary, which the Board's own documents describe numbering over 1100. The panel therefore finds the RPD erred in giving no weight to the letter from the Roma Self-Government.

The panel also finds the RPD erred in assessing the MA's psychiatric report, dated October 11, 2018. Specifically, the RPD erred in concluding two seeming inconsistencies in the report "go to the issue of the claimants' Roma identity". The RAD does not agree, as the apparent inconsistencies related to the MA's employment (whether he was a plumber or a sewage worker or cleaner) and a reference to an inter-racial relationship are not relevant nor determinative in establishing the appellants' Roma identity. In this regard, the panel also notes the MA relied on interpretation when his interview with the author of the report was conducted. Further, the evidence clearly indicates that two of the appellants' children are in inter-racial relationships. As such, the panel finds the RPD erred in drawing an adverse inference as to both of the appellants' identity based on two peripheral issues in the MA's report. Merits of the Claim

Having set aside the RPD's erroneous findings related to credibility and ethnicity, the panel has undertaken it own independent assessment of the evidence to provide a final determination of this claim, as follows.

The panel has carefully reviewed the evidence, including the audio recording of the RPD hearing. Both appellants testified (twice) as to their identity as Hungarian Roma, as well as about their allegations of persecution in Hungary. Their testimony was forthright and consistent. Their testimony was also consistent with their Basis of Claim forms and supporting documents, including medical notes from Hungary and Canada, a police report from Hungary in which the PA was threatened by an attacker yelling, "You're going to die, you Gipsy whore", a letter from the Roma Minority Government corroborating the appellants' Roma origin, and correspondence from individuals in Hungary.

The panel further notes the appellants' daughter "XXXX" and son "XXXX" fled to Canada in 2012. XXXX has since become a permanent resident of Canada. Most recently, in February 2019, XXXX received a positive refugee decision4 from the RPD. The RPD member accepted XXXX identity as a Hungarian Roma and concluded the discrimination and violent assaults that she suffered amounted to persecution. The RAD finds the RPD's findings in XXXX claim to be persuasive in assessing the appellants' (the parents of XXXX) claim, particularly with regards to their Roma identity, as well as their family's allegations of persecution.

Accordingly, having reviewed all of the evidence, the RAD finds the appellants have established, on a balance of probabilities, that as Roma from Forro (and then Budapest), they have been the victims of repeated incidents of discrimination, harassment, threats, and abuse of a variety of forms cumulatively amounting to persecution. In this regard, the appellants also provided examples of similarly situated Roma, including of their daughter, to corroborate their claims. The updated country documentation in the Board's most recent National Documentation Package also confirms the ongoing discrimination and attacks of Roma in Hungary. The documents describe that Roma also continue to be excluded from effective participation in social and economic life. Discrimination against Roma in access to housing and the failure to protect Roma and other minorities from hate crimes also continued.

The appellants also provided detailed accounts in their narratives and testimony describing their attempts (by various family members over the years) to obtain state protection to no avail. In this regard, the appellants also provided personal and country corroborating documents, which were not mentioned by the RPD at all. Accordingly, upon its own assessment of the evidence, including the updated country documentation, the RAD find the appellants, in their particular circumstances, have rebutted the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence that is both reliable and probative. The appellants provided multiple examples of their attempts to seek protection wherein it did not materialize for them. The RAD finds the appellants tested the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state and exhausted all courses of action to the extent that would be reasonably expected in their personal circumstances. In this regard, the panel also considered the updated country documentation indicating the situation for Roma has not improved and/or resulted in concrete examples of the effectiveness of state protection.

Having conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, the RAD finds that the appellants, in their personal circumstances, face discrimination which, cumulatively, rises to the level of a serious possibility of persecution in Hungary based upon their Roma ethnicity.

The RAD further finds the appellants have rebutted the presumption of state protection in their particular circumstances. The RAD similarly finds the appellants do not have a viable internal flight alternative as the problems facing Roma exist throughout the country, including the negative attitude toward Roma and widespread levels of discrimination that is prevalent and pervasive throughout Hungary.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act,5 the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own decision that the appellants are Convention refugees. The appeal is allowed. (signed) "D. Goff" D.
